# Keeno

> Keeno is a compiled, signal-based frontend framework. Components are `.kn` files with HTML-first JSX markup, a `<script>` block and a scoped `<style>` block. The compiler (via `@inflector/vite-plugin-keeno`) turns them into direct DOM code with fine-grained updates: no virtual DOM, no re-rendering components. Tooling is Bun (packages, scripts, `bun test`) plus Vite.

Rules that differ from React, Svelte and Vue, which models get wrong most often:

- **Reading state:** in `.kn` files, read a local state by name (`count`), not `count()` or `count.value`. Write with `count.set(v)`, never `count = v`.
- **Reserved members:** `x.set`, `x.get`, `x.peek`, `x.onUpdate`, `x.undo`, `x.redo`, `x.canUndo` and `x.canRedo` stay on the state. Any other member (`x.length`, `x.map`) reads the value.
- **Immutable updates:** `todos.set([...todos, item])`. In-place mutation (`todos.push`) does not update anything.
- **Computed values:** use `derived(() => …)`. Don't copy values between states in `update()`.
- **Shared stores:** in plain `.ts` files, states are plain objects (`s.get()`, `s.set()`), and imported stores stay that way in components.
- **Props:** `const { a, b = 1 } = props()` stays reactive. No `...rest`; use `const p = props()` instead.
- **Markup:** `class`, not `className` (both work). Use `onClick={fn}`, not `@click` or `on:click`. Two-way binding is `bind:value={state}`.
- **Lists:** `{list.map(item => <li key={item.id}>…</li>)}` is keyed. The callback must return JSX directly.
- **Lifecycle:** `init(fn)` runs after mount and its return value is cleanup. `update(fn)` runs when a value read inside `fn` changes (deps inferred by the compiler), and `update(fn, [a, b])` only when `a` or `b` changes; neither runs on mount. `destroy(fn)` runs on unmount.
- **State options:** `persist`, `url`, `history`, `equals`, `validate`, `debounce` and `throttle`.
- **Built-ins:** `ErrorBoundary`, `Await`, `Dynamic`, `Portal`, `Transition`, `lazy()` and `reparentable()` are imported from `@inflector/keeno`. Render props such as `fallback={(error, reset) => <p>…</p>}` and `fulfilled={(value) => …}` are functions.
- **Reparenting:** to move content between places without re-creating it, `const player = reparentable(() => <Video />)` and render `{player}` wherever it should be now. Use `keyedReparentable((id) => <Card id={id} />)` for items moving between lists. Imperatively: `player.moveTo(el)`, `player.remove()`, and `moveNode(node, parent)` for any DOM node.
- **Context:** `provide(Ctx, value)` and `inject(Ctx)` are called in `<script>`. To make the value reactive, provide a state. An injected state is a plain object, so use `.get()`.
- **Packages:** `@inflector/keeno` (runtime), `@inflector/keeno/server` (`renderToString`), `@inflector/keeno-router`, `@inflector/vite-plugin-keeno` and `@inflector/keeno-check`.

## Docs

<!-- file: docs/getting-started.md -->

# Getting started

Keeno is a compiled, signal-based frontend framework. You write components in `.kn` files: HTML-first markup with JSX-style `{expressions}`, a `<script>` block, and a scoped `<style>` block. The compiler turns each file into direct DOM code with fine-grained updates. There is no virtual DOM.

## Project setup

Keeno uses Bun for packages, scripts and tests, and Vite for the dev server and builds.

The quickest start is the project generator. It asks for a directory, a template (file-based routing or a single component) and whether to add Tailwind CSS:

```bash
bun create keeno my-app
```

To set a project up by hand instead:

```bash
bun add @inflector/keeno
bun add -d vite @inflector/vite-plugin-keeno
```

`vite.config.ts`:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import keeno from '@inflector/vite-plugin-keeno'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [keeno()],
})
```

`index.html`:

```html
<div id="app"></div>
<script type="module" src="/src/main.ts"></script>
```

`src/main.ts`:

```ts
import { mount } from '@inflector/keeno'
import App from './App.kn'

mount(App, document.getElementById('app')!)
```

`src/env.d.ts`, so plain `.ts` files can import `.kn` files:

```ts
declare module '*.kn' {
  const Component: import('@inflector/keeno').Component
  export default Component
}
```

Start the dev server with `bunx --bun vite` and build with `bunx --bun vite build`.

## A first component

```html App.kn
<script lang="ts">
  const count = state(0)
  const doubled = derived(() => count * 2)
</script>

<h1>Clicked {count} times ({doubled} doubled)</h1>
<button onClick={() => count.set(count + 1)}>+1</button>

<style>
  h1 { color: teal }
</style>
```

- `state(0)` creates a reactive value. Inside `.kn` files you read it by name (`count`) and write it with `count.set(…)`.
- `derived(…)` computes a value from other states and stays up to date automatically.
- `{count}` in the markup is a live text node: only that node changes when `count` changes.
- The `<style>` only applies to this component.

Continue with [Components](components.md), [Reactivity](reactivity.md) and [Templates](templates.md). To load data, see [async derived](reactivity.md#async-derived); for nested data you change in place, [`store()`](reactivity.md#store).

---

<!-- file: docs/components.md -->

# Components

A `.kn` file is one component. It has up to three parts, in any order:

- `<script>` or `<script lang="ts">`: runs once per component instance.
- Markup: everything outside `<script>` and `<style>`, parsed as JSX.
- `<style>`: CSS scoped to this component. See [Styles](styles.md).

Imports and TypeScript `type`/`interface` declarations in the script stay at module level. Everything else runs per instance. `export` is not allowed in the script.

## Props

Call `props()` and destructure it. Destructured props stay reactive, because the compiler rewrites `title` to a getter read (`$$props.title`).

```html Greeting.kn
<script lang="ts">
  const { name, greeting = 'Hello', onClose } = props<{ name: string; greeting?: string; onClose: () => void }>()
</script>

<p>{greeting}, {name}! <button onClick={() => onClose()}>×</button></p>
```

- Defaults use `??`: `greeting = 'Hello'` applies when the prop is `undefined` or `null`.
- A default that creates an object (`items = []`, `{}`, a function, `new …`) is evaluated once, when `props()` runs, so every read gets the same object.
- Renames work: `const { 'aria-label': label } = props()`.
- Rest destructuring (`...rest`) is not supported. Use `const p = props()` and read `p.x` instead.
- Callbacks are ordinary props.
- Never reassign a destructured prop: that is a compile error.
- The type argument also types the component for its parents: the editor and `keeno-check` report a missing required prop or a prop of the wrong type where the component is used, and complete prop names. Without a type argument, props are `any`.

Pass props like JSX. Dynamic values become getters, so the child sees updates:

```html Parent.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import Greeting from './Greeting.kn'
  const who = state('Ada')
</script>

<Greeting name={who} onClose={() => who.set('nobody')} />
```

Spread props work on components: `<Item {...item} selected={isSelected} />`. Later props win.

## Children

Nested content arrives as the `children` prop, a function that renders it. Type it as `Children` and put `{children}` where it should appear:

```html Card.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import type { Children } from '@inflector/keeno'
  const { title, children } = props<{ title: string; children?: Children }>()
</script>

<section>
  <h2>{title}</h2>
  {children}
</section>
```

```html UsesCard.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import Card from './Card.kn'
</script>

<Card title="Hi"><p>Card body</p></Card>
```

The parent writes `children` as nested markup, any number of nodes. Declare it as `children: Children` (not optional) to make content required.

## Lifecycle

| Helper | When it runs |
|---|---|
| `init(fn)` | Once, after the component's DOM is inserted. If `fn` returns a function, that runs on destroy. |
| `update(fn)` | Whenever a state, derived, prop or other reactive value read inside `fn` changes, not on mount (the compiler infers the deps; use `init` for the first run). A returned function is cleanup before the next run and on destroy. |
| `update(fn, [a, b])` | Only when `a` or `b` changes, not on mount. The array holds the states themselves. A returned function is cleanup. |
| `destroy(fn)` | When the component unmounts. |
| `x.onUpdate((old, next) => …)` | Synchronously on every real change of `x`. Removed automatically on destroy; also returns an unsubscribe function. |

For setup tied to one element that you'd reuse elsewhere (listeners, observers, third-party widgets), a [directive](directives.md) (`use:name={value}`) is often simpler than a `ref` plus `init`.

Order:
- Children mount before their parents.
- Within a component, `init` and `update` run in declaration order.
- On unmount, children are destroyed before parents, and callbacks run in registration order.

```html Clock.kn
<script lang="ts">
  const now = state(new Date())
  init(() => {
    const id = setInterval(() => now.set(new Date()), 1000)
    return () => clearInterval(id)
  })
  update(() => {
    document.title = now.toLocaleTimeString()
  })
</script>

<time>{now.toLocaleTimeString()}</time>
```

## Mounting

`mount(Component, target, props?)` renders at the end of `target`, runs the `init` and `update` jobs, and returns `{ destroy() }`.

---

<!-- file: docs/reactivity.md -->

# Reactivity

Keeno tracks reads of states and deriveds, and re-runs exactly the code that depends on them. There is no virtual DOM and no component re-rendering.

## state

```ts
const count = state(0)
```

In a `.kn` file:

| You write | It means |
|---|---|
| `count` | Read the value (tracked) |
| `count.set(v)` | Write. Does nothing if the value is equal (`Object.is` by default) |
| `count.peek()` | Read without tracking |
| `count.get()` | Explicit tracked read |
| `count.onUpdate((old, next) => …)` | Synchronous listener for real changes |
| `count.undo()`, `count.redo()`, `count.canUndo`, `count.canRedo` | History, with the `history` option |
| `count.foo` (anything else) | `count.get().foo` |

To call a method of the value that shares a reserved name, go through `get()`: `map.get().set(k, v)`.

States are immutable by convention. Update arrays and objects with a new value:

```ts
todos.set([...todos, newTodo])
todos.set(todos.filter((t) => t.id !== id))
todos.set(todos.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)))
```

Mutating in place (`todos.push(x)`) does not trigger updates.

Writes are synchronous: the value changes immediately and `onUpdate` listeners run right away. DOM updates and `update(fn)` re-runs are batched in a microtask.

Reassigning a state variable (`count = 5`) is a compile error. Use `count.set(5)`.

## derived

`derived(fn)` is a computed, read-only signal. It recomputes only when something it read changes, and it is always current, even when read synchronously right after a write.

```html Cart.kn
<script lang="ts">
  const price = state(10)
  const qty = state(2)
  const total = derived(() => price * qty)
  const expensive = derived(() => total > 100)

  function more() {
    qty.set(qty + 1)
    console.log(total) // already updated
  }
</script>

<p>{qty} × {price} = {total}</p>
{expensive && <p class="warn">That's a lot</p>}
<button onClick={more}>more</button>
```

- Use `derived` instead of copying values into other states inside `update()`. That pattern goes stale or loops; this one cannot.
- Code that reads a derived only re-runs when its value actually changes. In the example above, `{expensive && …}` re-renders only when `total` crosses 100.
- `derived(fn, { equals })` takes a custom equality function.
- A derived reads like a state, with `get`, `peek` and `onUpdate`. It has no `set`, and `bind:` on a derived is a compile error.
- A derived that depends on itself throws.

## Async derived

Give `derived` an async function and it holds the resolved value. Render it inside [`<Loading>`](built-ins.md#loading), which shows a fallback until the first value arrives:

```html User.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { Loading, pending } from '@inflector/keeno'
  const { userId } = props<{ userId: number }>()

  const user = derived(async () => {
    const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${userId}`)
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`)
    return res.json() as Promise<{ name: string; email: string }>
  })
</script>

<Loading fallback={() => <p>Loading…</p>}>
  <h1>{user.name}</h1>
  <p>{user.email}</p>
  {pending(() => user) && <small>refreshing…</small>}
  <button onClick={() => user.refresh()}>Reload</button>
</Loading>
```

- It reads like any derived: `{user.name}` in markup, `user` in other deriveds. A derived that reads an async one waits for it too.
- When something it read changes (`userId` above), it runs again. The current value stays on screen until the new one arrives, and a result from a run that was replaced in the meantime is ignored.
- `user.refresh()` runs it again on demand, with the same keep-the-old-value behavior.
- `pending(() => user)` is true while a run is in flight, including re-runs. It is reactive.
- A rejection or a thrown error goes to the closest `<ErrorBoundary>`.
- Only the reads **before the first `await`** are tracked. Read the states you depend on at the top of the function.
- Read async values in markup or in other deriveds, not at the top of a component's `<script>`: there, a value that isn't ready yet stops the component from being created.

### Aborting requests

The function receives a `signal` that is aborted when a newer run starts or the component is destroyed. Pass it to `fetch` to cancel requests that are no longer needed:

```ts
const results = derived(async ({ signal }) => {
  const res = await fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`, { signal })
  return res.json()
})
```

With [server rendering](ssr.md), the value the server fetched is sent to the browser and reused, and a `fetch` given `signal` is skipped during hydration.

## update vs onUpdate vs derived

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| A value computed from other values | `derived` |
| A side effect (DOM, storage, network) when values change | `update(fn)` or `update(fn, [deps])` |
| React synchronously to each change of one state, with the old value | `x.onUpdate` |

## Shared stores in plain .ts files

Outside `.kn` files, states are plain objects, so you call `.get()` and `.set()` yourself:

```ts
// store.ts
import { derived, state } from '@inflector/keeno'

export const user = state<{ name: string } | null>(null, { persist: 'user' })
export const isLoggedIn = derived(() => user.get() !== null)
```

Only states and deriveds declared in the `.kn` file itself are unwrapped. An imported state is used as `user.get()` and `user.set(…)` in components too.

## store

`store(obj)` is a deep reactive object for nested data. Read and change it like a plain object: assignments, `push`, `splice`, `delete`. Only the code that read a changed property re-runs.

```html Todos.kn
<script lang="ts">
  const todos = store({
    draft: '',
    items: [] as { id: number; title: string; done: boolean }[],
  })
  const left = derived(() => todos.items.filter((t) => !t.done).length)

  function add() {
    todos.items.push({ id: Date.now(), title: todos.draft, done: false })
    todos.draft = ''
  }
</script>

<input bind:value={todos.draft} />
<button onClick={add}>Add</button>
<ul>
  {todos.items.map((t) => (
    <li key={t.id}>
      <input type="checkbox" bind:checked={t.done} />
      {t.title}
    </li>
  ))}
</ul>
<p>{left} left</p>
```

- Checking one todo re-runs only what reads that todo's `done` (its checkbox and `left`). The list and the other rows stay as they are.
- A store isn't unwrapped like a state: you use it directly, in `.kn` and `.ts` files alike. It works the same when imported from a shared module.
- `bind:value` and `bind:checked` work on store properties, such as `bind:value={form.user.email}`.
- Plain objects and arrays inside a store are reactive too. Other values (Dates, Maps, Sets, class instances) are stored as they are: replace them to trigger updates.
- Changes made in the same tick are batched, like state writes.
- `snapshot(todos)` returns a plain deep copy, for `JSON.stringify`, logging or sending to a server. Used in a derived or in markup, it re-runs on any change inside the store.
- `reconcile(todos.items, fresh)` updates a store to match new data while changing only what differs. Array items with the same `id` (or another `key` option) are kept and updated in place. Use it to apply fresh server data without re-rendering rows that didn't change.

Use `state` for single values and data you replace as a whole, and `store` for nested data that you change in place.

## Batching and flush

All work runs in one microtask, in this order: stale deriveds, DOM updates, mount jobs (`init` and the first `update` runs), then `update` re-runs. `flush()` from `@inflector/keeno` runs pending work synchronously, which is handy in tests.

See [State options](state-options.md) for persistence, URL sync, undo/redo, validation and debouncing.

---

<!-- file: docs/state-options.md -->

# State options

`state(value, options)` accepts these options. They combine freely, except `debounce` with `throttle`.

| Option | Type | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `equals` | `(a, b) => boolean` | Replaces `Object.is` to decide whether a write is a change. |
| `validate` | `(next, prev) => value` | Coerces or rejects writes. Return `prev` to reject. |
| `persist` | `string` | Saves to `localStorage` under this key and syncs across tabs. |
| `url` | `string` or `{ param, replace? }` | Two-way sync with a query parameter. Back and forward work. |
| `history` | `number` | Keeps this many past values for `undo()` and `redo()`. |
| `debounce` | `number` (ms) | Applies a write only after writes stop for this long. |
| `throttle` | `number` (ms) | Applies at most one write per interval: the first one now, the last one at the end. |
| `save` | `(next, prev, { signal }) => unknown` | Sends each change to a server. Writes apply at once and roll back if the save fails. |

## equals

```ts
import { deepEqual } from '@inflector/keeno'

const filters = state({ tags: [] as string[] }, { equals: deepEqual })
filters.set({ tags: [] }) // no change, nothing re-runs
```

`deepEqual` compares primitives, arrays, plain objects and dates structurally.

## validate

`validate(next, prev)` runs on every write, and also on the initial value and on values loaded from storage or the URL. Return the value to store. Return `prev` to reject the write.

```ts
const volume = state(50, { validate: (v) => Math.min(100, Math.max(0, v)) })
const age = state(30, { validate: (v, prev) => (Number.isInteger(v) && v >= 0 ? v : prev) })
```

With `bind:value`, the input shows the stored value after a coerced or rejected write.

## persist

```ts
const todos = state<Todo[]>([], { persist: 'todos' })
```

- On creation, the saved value (JSON) replaces the initial value, after `validate`. Unreadable data is ignored.
- Every change is saved, and other tabs with a state on the same key receive it through `BroadcastChannel`.
- Values must be JSON-serializable. Writing `undefined` removes the key.

## url

```ts
const page = state(1, { url: 'page' }) // ?page=2
const q = state('', { url: { param: 'q', replace: true }, debounce: 300 })
```

- **Reading:** the initial value comes from the query parameter, parsed according to the default's type:
  - strings as-is
  - numbers with `Number` (an invalid number falls back to the default)
  - booleans from `true`, `1` or an empty value
  - anything else as JSON
- **Writing:** writes update the query. All URL states changed in the same tick produce a single history entry. When the value equals the default, the parameter is removed.
- **Back and forward:** both restore earlier values without adding entries.
- **`replace: true`:** uses `history.replaceState`, for values like a search box that shouldn't fill the history.

## history

```html Editor.kn
<script lang="ts">
  const text = state('', { history: 100 })
</script>

<textarea bind:value={text}></textarea>
<button disabled={!text.canUndo} onClick={() => text.undo()}>Undo</button>
<button disabled={!text.canRedo} onClick={() => text.redo()}>Redo</button>
```

- Each change pushes the old value, and the stack keeps the last `history` values. Because updates are immutable, this stores references and doesn't copy.
- A new write clears the redo stack.
- `canUndo` and `canRedo` are reactive.
- `undo()` and `redo()` notify like normal writes, so persistence and URL sync follow.
- Without the option, `undo()` and `redo()` do nothing.

## debounce and throttle

```ts
const search = state('', { debounce: 300 })
update(() => {
  fetchResults(search) // runs 300 ms after typing stops
})
```

- **debounce:** the value changes only when writes stop for that long.
- **throttle:** the first write applies immediately, and later writes in the window collapse into one at the end.
- **Inputs:** with `bind:value` the input keeps what the user types while a write is pending.
- **Unmount:** pending writes are dropped when the component unmounts.

## save

`save` makes a state optimistic: a write shows at once, then `save(next, prev, { signal })` sends it. If the returned promise rejects, the state goes back to the last saved value and the error goes to the nearest `<ErrorBoundary>`.

```html TodoList.kn
<script lang="ts">
  const todos = state<Todo[]>(initial, {
    save: (next, prev, { signal }) =>
      fetch('/api/todos', { method: 'PUT', body: JSON.stringify(next), signal }).then((r) => {
        if (!r.ok) throw new Error('Could not save')
      }),
  })
</script>

<button onClick={() => todos.set([...todos, { id: Date.now(), title: 'New' }])}>Add</button>
{pending(() => todos) && <small>Saving…</small>}
```

- **Concurrency:** a newer write aborts the older save (pass `signal` to `fetch`). Only the latest save decides the outcome.
- **Server response:** resolve with a value to replace the state with it, for example the saved record with its new id. Resolving with `undefined` keeps the state as it is.
- **pending:** `pending(() => todos)` is true while a save is in flight, and `bind:value` doesn't overwrite what the user is typing during it.
- **Other options:** `save` runs after `debounce`/`throttle`, and also for `undo()`/`redo()`. Values loaded from storage, the URL or another tab don't trigger it.

---

<!-- file: docs/templates.md -->

# Templates

Markup is JSX, written HTML-first: use `class` and `for` (`className` and `htmlFor` also work). JSX whitespace rules apply. Write `{'>'}` or `&gt;` for a literal `>` in text. HTML comments `<!-- -->` are allowed in markup.

## Expressions

`{expr}` is a live text node or attribute. It updates when the states it reads change, and nothing else is touched.

```html Profile.kn
<script lang="ts">
  const user = state({ name: 'Ada', avatar: '/ada.png' })
</script>

<img src={user.avatar} alt={user.name} />
<p title={`User ${user.name}`}>{user.name}</p>
```

Attribute values: `null`, `undefined` and `false` remove the attribute, and `true` sets it empty. `value`, `checked` and `selected` are set as DOM properties.

## Conditionals

```html Status.kn
<script lang="ts">
  const count = state(0)
  const user = state<{ name: string } | null>(null)
</script>

{count > 5 && <p class="warn">big!</p>}
{user ? <p>Hi {user.name}</p> : <button>Log in</button>}
{user || <i>anonymous</i>}
```

- **Re-rendering:** a branch is created or destroyed only when its condition changes truthiness. `{count > 5 && <p/>}` keeps the same `<p>` while `count` goes from 6 to 7.
- **Falsy numbers:** as in JS, `{0 && <X/>}` renders `0`.

## Lists

```html List.kn
<script lang="ts">
  const todos = state([{ id: 1, text: 'Write docs', done: false }])
</script>

<ul>
  {todos.map((t, i) => (
    <li key={t.id} class={{ done: t.done }}>{i + 1}. {t.text}</li>
  ))}
</ul>
```

- **Keyed reconciliation:** `X.map(item => <el key={…}>)` compiles to keyed reconciliation. Adding, removing or reordering items touches only the affected rows.
- **Item changes:** when an item changes but keeps its key, its row updates in place, and its DOM, focus and child state survive.
- **Callback shape:** the callback must be an arrow or function whose body is JSX, or a block that only returns JSX. The parameter can be an identifier or a simple destructuring (`({ id, text }) => …`).
- **Missing key:** without `key`, the item itself is the key.
- **Other `.map` calls:** a `.map` that doesn't return JSX is a normal JS expression.

## Events

`onClick={fn}`, `onInput={fn}`, `onKeyDown={fn}` and so on: the name is lowercased after `on`, so `onDblClick` listens to `dblclick`. Handlers receive the DOM event.

```html Form.kn
<script lang="ts">
  const sent = state(false)
</script>

<form onSubmit={(e) => { e.preventDefault(); sent.set(true) }}>
  <button>Send</button>
</form>
```

## Two-way binding

`bind:value={myState}` (inputs, textareas, selects) and `bind:checked={myState}` (checkboxes) take the state itself:

```html Settings.kn
<script lang="ts">
  const name = state('')
  const volume = state(5)
  const dark = state(false)
</script>

<input bind:value={name} />
<input type="number" bind:value={volume} />
<input type="checkbox" bind:checked={dark} />
<p>{name} {volume} {dark ? 'dark' : 'light'}</p>
```

Number and range inputs store numbers. Binding a prop or a derived is a compile error.

## Element refs

`ref()` creates a reference; `ref={myRef}` points it at an element. `myRef.current` is the element, or `null` before mount and after the element is removed. Reading `current` is reactive, so `update` re-runs when the element appears or goes away:

```html Search.kn
<script lang="ts">
  const input = ref<HTMLInputElement>()

  init(() => input.current?.focus())
</script>

<input ref={input} />
```

`ref` also takes a function, called with the element on mount and with `null` on removal: `<canvas ref={(el) => (canvas = el)} />`. Refs work on DOM elements only.

For a behavior you'd reuse on many elements, such as a tooltip, click-outside or autosize, write a [directive](directives.md) instead.

## Directives

`use:name={value}` adds a reusable DOM behavior to an element, such as a tooltip, click-outside or autosize. A directive is a plain function, `(el, value) => cleanup`. It runs once the element is in the document, runs again when the value changes, and cleans up when the element is removed:

```html
<textarea use:autofocus use:autosize bind:value={note}></textarea>
<div class="menu" use:clickOutside={() => open.set(false)}>…</div>
```

See [Directives](directives.md) for writing them, reactive values, type checking and more examples.

## class

`class` accepts a string, an array (falsy entries skipped, nested arrays allowed) or an object of `name: condition`:

```html Button.kn
<script lang="ts">
  const active = state(false)
  const size = state('big')
</script>

<button class={['btn', active && 'on', { [size]: true }]} onClick={() => active.set(!active)}>Toggle</button>
```

The component's scope class is always kept.

## Spread

Spread works on components and on DOM elements. Attributes apply in order, and later ones win:

```html Field.kn
<script lang="ts">
  const attrs = state({ placeholder: 'Email', type: 'email', required: true })
  const touched = state(false)
</script>

<input {...attrs} class={['field', touched && 'touched']} onBlur={() => touched.set(true)} />
```

Spread objects can include `class`, `onX` event handlers and any attribute. When the spread value changes, removed keys are cleared and changed handlers are swapped.

## SVG

Inline `<svg>` works as in HTML. Conditionals, lists and components inside it render SVG elements:

```html Dot.kn
<script lang="ts">
  const { x, y } = props()
</script>

<circle cx={x} cy={y} r="4" />
```

```html Chart.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import Dot from './Dot.kn'
  const points = state([{ id: 1, x: 10, y: 20 }])
  const grid = state(true)
</script>

<svg viewBox="0 0 100 100">
  {grid && <line x1="0" y1="90" x2="100" y2="90" />}
  <g>{points.map((p) => <Dot key={p.id} x={p.x} y={p.y} />)}</g>
</svg>
```

- **SVG roots:** a component or branch whose root is an SVG-only element (`<circle>`, `<g>`, `<path>`, `<text>`, …) is created in the SVG namespace.
- **Shared tag names:** `<a>`, `<title>`, `<style>` and `<script>` exist in both HTML and SVG. Inside `<svg>` in the same file they are SVG. As the root of a separate component they are HTML, so wrap them in a `<g>`.
- **`<foreignObject>`:** its content is HTML again.

## Tables

Write tables with their full structure. Rows go in `<tbody>`, `<thead>` or `<tfoot>`, and cells go in `<tr>`:

```html Stock.kn
<script lang="ts">
  const items = state([{ id: 1, name: 'apples', qty: 3 }])
</script>

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr><th>Name</th><th>Qty</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    {items.map((i) => (
      <tr key={i.id}><td>{i.name}</td><td>{i.qty}</td></tr>
    ))}
  </tbody>
</table>
```

- **Compile errors:** HTML parsers rewrite misplaced table content. `<table><tr>` gets an implied `<tbody>`, and text or a `<div>` inside a `<tr>` is moved out of the table. Keeno reports these as compile errors instead of rendering a different tree, for example: `<tr> cannot be a direct child of <table>: the HTML parser would insert a <tbody> and break the template. Wrap it in <tbody> (or <thead>/<tfoot>).`
- **Allowed children:** `<table>` takes `<caption>`, `<colgroup>`, `<thead>`, `<tbody>` and `<tfoot>`. `<thead>`, `<tbody>` and `<tfoot>` take `<tr>`. `<tr>` takes `<td>` and `<th>`. `<colgroup>` takes `<col>`. `{expressions}`, components, whitespace, `<template>`, `<script>` and `<style>` are allowed anywhere.
- **Row components:** a component can have `<tr>` or `<td>` as its root.

## Components

A capitalized tag is a component: `<Item text={t.text} onSave={save} />`. Dynamic props are passed as getters, so the child stays in sync. See [Components](components.md).

---

<!-- file: docs/directives.md -->

# Directives

A directive is a reusable DOM behavior: a tooltip, closing a menu on an outside click, growing a textarea, watching when an element scrolls into view. You write it once as a plain function, then put it on any element with `use:name={value}`.

```html Inbox.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { tooltip } from './directives'
  const unread = state(3)
</script>

<button use:tooltip={`${unread} unread messages`} onClick={() => unread.set(unread + 1)}>
  Inbox ({unread})
</button>
```

## Writing a directive

A directive receives the element and the value, and can return a cleanup function:

```ts
// directives.ts
import type { Directive } from '@inflector/keeno'

export const tooltip: Directive<HTMLElement, string> = (el, text) => {
  const tip = document.createElement('div')
  tip.className = 'tooltip'
  tip.textContent = text
  const show = () => {
    const r = el.getBoundingClientRect()
    tip.style.left = `${r.left + r.width / 2}px`
    tip.style.top = `${r.top - 6}px`
    document.body.append(tip)
  }
  const hide = () => tip.remove()
  el.addEventListener('pointerenter', show)
  el.addEventListener('pointerleave', hide)
  return () => {
    hide()
    el.removeEventListener('pointerenter', show)
    el.removeEventListener('pointerleave', hide)
  }
}
```

- `Directive<ElementType, ValueType>` types both arguments. Both are optional: `Directive` alone is `(el: HTMLElement) => …`.
- The directive runs once the element is in the document, like `init`, so it can measure the element, focus it or attach observers.
- The cleanup runs when the element is removed: its component is destroyed, its `{cond && …}` turns false, or its list row goes away.

## Using directives

```html Note.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { autofocus, autosize, clickOutside } from './directives'
  const open = state(false)
  const note = state('')
</script>

<button onClick={() => open.set(true)}>Write a note</button>
{open && (
  <div class="popover" use:clickOutside={() => open.set(false)}>
    <textarea use:autofocus use:autosize bind:value={note}></textarea>
  </div>
)}
```

- `use:name` refers to `name` in scope: an import, a function declared in the `<script>`, a prop or a state holding a function.
- Without a value (`use:autosize`), the directive receives `undefined`.
- An element can have several directives. They run in the order they're written.
- Directives work on DOM elements only; on a component they're a compile error. The name must be a JavaScript identifier (`use:clickOutside`, not `use:click-outside`), and the value an expression (`use:tooltip={'Save'}`, not `use:tooltip="Save"`).

## Reactive values

The value is tracked like any expression in markup. When a state it reads changes, the cleanup runs and the directive runs again with the new value. Above, the tooltip follows `unread`.

- Reads **inside** the directive aren't tracked: only the value expression (and the directive itself, when it's a prop or a state) re-runs it.
- For a value that changes often, a directive can accept a getter instead, so it isn't set up again each time: `use:tooltip={() => `${unread} unread`}` passes a function that never changes, and the directive calls it when the tooltip opens.
- A value that reads an [async derived](reactivity.md#async-derived) waits inside `<Loading>` like the rest of the markup.

## More examples

**Click outside**, to close menus and popovers:

```ts
export const clickOutside: Directive<HTMLElement, () => void> = (el, onOutside) => {
  const handler = (e: PointerEvent) => !el.contains(e.target as Node) && onOutside()
  document.addEventListener('pointerdown', handler, true)
  return () => document.removeEventListener('pointerdown', handler, true)
}
```

**Autosize and autofocus:**

```ts
export const autosize: Directive<HTMLTextAreaElement> = (el) => {
  const fit = () => {
    el.style.height = 'auto'
    el.style.height = `${el.scrollHeight}px`
  }
  fit()
  el.addEventListener('input', fit)
  return () => el.removeEventListener('input', fit)
}

export const autofocus: Directive = (el) => el.focus()
```

**In view**, for infinite scroll, lazy images and scroll animations:

```ts
export const inView: Directive<Element, (visible: boolean) => void> = (el, onChange) => {
  const io = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => onChange(entry!.isIntersecting), { rootMargin: '200px' })
  io.observe(el)
  return () => io.disconnect()
}
```

```html Feed.kn
<ul>{posts.map((p) => <li key={p.id}>{p.title}</li>)}</ul>
<div use:inView={(visible) => visible && loadMore()}>Loading…</div>
```

**Long press:**

```ts
export const longpress: Directive<HTMLElement, () => void> = (el, onPress) => {
  let timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined
  const down = () => (timer = setTimeout(onPress, 500))
  const up = () => clearTimeout(timer)
  el.addEventListener('pointerdown', down)
  el.addEventListener('pointerup', up)
  el.addEventListener('pointerleave', up)
  return () => {
    up()
    el.removeEventListener('pointerdown', down)
    el.removeEventListener('pointerup', up)
    el.removeEventListener('pointerleave', up)
  }
}
```

**A local directive** that reads the component's states:

```html Card.kn
<script lang="ts">
  const accent = state('#f97316')
  const outline = (el: HTMLElement, on: boolean) => {
    if (!on) return
    el.style.outline = `2px solid ${accent.peek()}`
    return () => (el.style.outline = '')
  }
  const selected = state(false)
</script>

<section use:outline={selected} onClick={() => selected.set(!selected)}>…</section>
```

## Directives vs. ref and init

A [ref](templates.md#element-refs) plus `init` does the same job for one element in one component:

```html
<script lang="ts">
  const input = ref<HTMLInputElement>()
  init(() => input.current?.focus())
</script>

<input ref={input} />
```

Use a directive when the behavior is reused. It works on any element in any component, several of them combine on one element, its value is reactive, and it cleans up after itself, with no ref or lifecycle code in the components that use it.

## Type checking

In the editor and in `keeno-check`, each `use:` is checked against the directive:

- **The value** must match the directive's value type. `use:tooltip={{ txt: 'Save' }}` is an error when `tooltip` expects `{ text: string }`.
- **The element** must match its element type. `use:autosize` on an `<input>` is an error because `autosize` expects a `<textarea>`. A directive typed for `HTMLElement` (the default) works on any element.
- **A required value** can't be left out: `use:tooltip` alone is an error when `tooltip` needs a value.

Go to definition and hover work on the directive's name.

## Server rendering

Directives don't run during [server rendering](ssr.md), because they need a live DOM. They run when the page hydrates in the browser.

## Errors

An error thrown by a directive, or while it re-runs, goes to the closest [`<ErrorBoundary>`](built-ins.md#errorboundary). Using something that isn't a function (`use:tooltip` where `tooltip` is a string) throws `use:tooltip needs a function`.

## Publishing directives

A directive is a plain function, so a package can export it with no component wrapper and no setup:

```ts
// @acme/tooltip
import type { Directive } from '@inflector/keeno'

export interface TooltipOptions {
  text: string
  placement?: 'top' | 'bottom'
}

export const tooltip: Directive<HTMLElement, TooltipOptions> = (el, options) => {
  // …
}
```

Users import it and write `use:tooltip={{ text: 'Save' }}` on their own markup, combined with any other directives. Keep setup cheap, since a value change runs it again, and always return a cleanup that removes every listener, observer and node the directive added.

---

<!-- file: docs/styles.md -->

# Styles

The `<style>` block of a component is scoped to it.

- **Scope class:** each component gets a class `keeno-<hash of the file path>`. Every element in its markup gets that class, and every compound selector in its CSS gets it too: `h1 { … }` becomes `h1.keeno-1a2b3c4d { … }`, and `ul > li.done` becomes `ul.keeno-… > li.done.keeno-…`.
- **Escape hatch:** `:global(...)` is left as written: `:global(body) { margin: 0 }` and `:global(.dark) h1 { … }`.
- **Pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements:** the scope class goes before them (`a:hover` becomes `a.keeno-…:hover`).
- **At-rules:** `@media` rules are scoped. `@keyframes` steps are not.

```html Panel.kn
<div class="panel"><h2>Title</h2></div>

<style>
  .panel { padding: 1rem }
  h2 { color: teal }              /* only this component's h2 */
  :global(body) { margin: 0 }     /* global */
</style>
```

Styles don't leak between components, and parent styles don't reach into children. Dynamic `class` values keep the scope class. The router's `<Link>` is an exception: its `<a>` gets the scope class of the component that renders it, as if you had written the `<a>` yourself.

## Tailwind CSS

Keeno works with Tailwind CSS v4. Add `@tailwindcss/vite` next to the Keeno plugin and import Tailwind from a stylesheet:

```bash
bun add -d tailwindcss @tailwindcss/vite
```

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import tailwindcss from '@tailwindcss/vite'
import keeno from '@inflector/vite-plugin-keeno'

export default defineConfig({ plugins: [keeno(), tailwindcss()] })
```

```css
/* src/app.css, imported once from main.ts */
@import 'tailwindcss';
```

- **Utilities in markup:** Tailwind scans `.kn` files, so classes in `class="…"` and in `class={[…]}` arrays and ternaries are generated. Write class names in full (`'bg-red-500'`, not `` `bg-${color}-500` ``).
- **Directives in `<style>`:** `@apply`, `@variant`, `theme()`, `--theme()`, `--spacing()` and `--alpha()` work in component styles, and the result stays scoped.
- **No `@reference` needed:** a component style that uses Tailwind gets `@reference` to your main stylesheet added for you. That's the shallowest `.css` file in the project that imports `tailwindcss`, so your `@theme` tokens are available. Write your own `@reference` to choose another file, or set `keeno({ tailwind: { reference: 'src/app.css' } })`.
- **Not scoped:** rules inside `@utility`, `@theme` and `@custom-variant`, which define global things.

```html Button.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import type { Children } from '@inflector/keeno'
  const { children } = props<{ children: Children }>()
</script>

<button class="btn">{children}</button>

<style>
  .btn {
    @apply rounded-lg bg-sky-600 px-4 py-2 text-white;
    @variant hover {
      @apply bg-sky-700;
    }
  }
</style>
```

This is on whenever `@tailwindcss/vite` is in the plugins. Turn it off with `keeno({ tailwind: false })`. For editor support, see [Tooling](tooling.md#tailwind-css-intellisense). `examples/todo` is a complete app.

## Virtual CSS module

The CSS is served as a virtual module (`Foo.kn?keeno&type=style&lang.css`). Vite injects it in dev with hot updates and extracts it in builds.

---

<!-- file: docs/context.md -->

# Context

Context passes a value from a component to everything rendered inside it, however deep, without threading it through props. Typical uses are a theme, the current user or a store.

## Creating a context

`createContext(defaultValue)` creates a context. Give it a type, and the default that `inject` returns when no component provided a value:

```ts
// theme.ts
import { createContext } from '@inflector/keeno'

export const Theme = createContext<'light' | 'dark'>('light')
```

## Providing a value

A component provides a value with `provide(context, value)`:

```html App.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { provide, state } from '@inflector/keeno'
  import { Theme } from './theme'
  import Toolbar from './Toolbar.kn'
  const theme = state<'light' | 'dark'>('dark')
  provide(Theme, theme)
</script>

<button onClick={() => theme.set(theme === 'dark' ? 'light' : 'dark')}>Switch</button>
<Toolbar />
```

## Reading a value

Any component inside it reads the value with `inject(context)`:

```html Toolbar.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { inject } from '@inflector/keeno'
  import { Theme } from './theme'
  const theme = inject(Theme)
</script>

<nav class={theme}>…</nav>
```

## Rules

- `inject` returns the value from the closest component that provided one, or else the context's default value. `createContext()` without a default gives `undefined`.
- Call `provide` and `inject` in the `<script>` block, while the component is being created. Event handlers, timers and promise callbacks run outside the component tree, so `inject` there only sees the default.

## Reactive values

Context values are reactive. In a `.kn` file:

- `provide(Theme, theme)` with a state or a derived provides the state itself, not its current value.
- `provide(User, { name, role })`, or any other expression that reads states or props, is provided as `derived(() => …)`, so it follows them.
- `const theme = inject(Theme)` reads like a state: `{theme}` and `theme.foo` are tracked. When a state was provided, `theme.set(…)` writes to it. Other values are read-only.

In a `.ts` file, `inject` returns exactly what was provided: a state or derived (call `.get()`), or a plain value.

## Where context reaches

Context reaches everything a component renders: children passed as markup, keyed list rows, `<Portal>` content and components loaded with `lazy()`.

---

<!-- file: docs/built-ins.md -->

# Built-in components

`@inflector/keeno` exports a few components for things plain markup can't express: catching errors, waiting for async data and promises, loading code on demand, rendering elsewhere in the page, moving live content around without re-creating it, and animating elements in and out. Import them like any component.

## ErrorBoundary

An error thrown while a component renders, updates or mounts (including inside `init` and `update`) goes to the closest `<ErrorBoundary>`, which shows `fallback` instead of its children:

```html App.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { ErrorBoundary } from '@inflector/keeno'
  import Chart from './Chart.kn'
</script>

<ErrorBoundary
  fallback={(error, reset) => (
    <div class="error">
      <p>Something went wrong: {String(error)}</p>
      <button onClick={reset}>Try again</button>
    </div>
  )}
  onError={(error) => console.error(error)}
>
  <Chart />
</ErrorBoundary>
```

- `fallback` is either content (`fallback="Failed"`) or a function of the error and `reset`. `reset()` renders the children again from scratch.
- `onError` is called once for each caught error, which makes it a good place to report to an error tracker.
- An error thrown by the fallback itself goes to the next boundary up.
- Errors in event handlers, timers and promise callbacks are **not** caught, because they don't happen while rendering. Handle them where they happen, or store them in a state and throw it while rendering.
- Without a boundary, the error is thrown from `mount()`, or reported as an uncaught error if it happens during a later update. The rest of the app keeps working.

A `derived` that throws passes the error on to whatever reads it, and it recovers on its own once its sources change.

## Loading

`<Loading>` shows `fallback` while an [async derived](reactivity.md#async-derived) read by its children has no value yet:

```html Profile.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { Loading } from '@inflector/keeno'
  const user = derived(async () => (await fetch('/api/me')).json())
</script>

<Loading fallback={() => <Spinner />}>
  <h1>{user.name}</h1>
  <Settings />
</Loading>
```

- The children are created once. While the fallback shows they stay alive off-screen, so `<Settings />` keeps its state.
- Only the first load shows the fallback. Re-runs keep the current content; use `pending()` to show that something is refreshing.
- Nested `<Loading>` boundaries each wait for what is read inside them.
- Errors pass through to the closest `<ErrorBoundary>`, which can sit inside or outside it.
- An async value read outside any `<Loading>` renders nothing until it resolves, with a warning in development.

## Await

`<Await>` renders the states of a promise. For data that depends on states or props, an [async derived](reactivity.md#async-derived) with `<Loading>` is usually simpler.

```html User.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { Await } from '@inflector/keeno'
  const { id } = props<{ id: number }>()
  const load = (id: number) => fetch(`/api/users/${id}`).then((r) => r.json() as Promise<{ name: string }>)
</script>

<Await
  promise={load(id)}
  pending={() => <p>Loading…</p>}
  fulfilled={(user) => <h1>{user.name}</h1>}
  rejected={(error) => <p class="error">{String(error)}</p>}
/>
```

- When `id` changes, `load(id)` runs again and `pending` shows until the new promise settles. Results from a promise that was replaced in the meantime are ignored.
- Without `rejected`, a rejection goes to the closest `<ErrorBoundary>`.
- A plain value instead of a promise renders `fulfilled` right away.

## lazy

`lazy()` loads a component when it is first rendered, so it ends up in its own chunk:

```ts
import { lazy } from '@inflector/keeno'

export const Chart = lazy(() => import('./Chart.kn'), { pending: () => 'Loading chart…' })
```

Use `Chart` like any other component. `Chart.preload()` starts loading earlier, for example on hover. If loading fails, the error goes to the closest `<ErrorBoundary>`, and rendering the component again (for example with `reset()`) retries the load.

## Dynamic

`<Dynamic>` renders whatever component is in its `component` prop and passes it the other props. It creates a new instance when `component` changes:

```html Tabs.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { Dynamic } from '@inflector/keeno'
  import Profile from './Profile.kn'
  import Settings from './Settings.kn'
  const tabs = { profile: Profile, settings: Settings }
  const tab = state<keyof typeof tabs>('profile')
</script>

<button onClick={() => tab.set('profile')}>Profile</button>
<button onClick={() => tab.set('settings')}>Settings</button>
<Dynamic component={tabs[tab]} user="ada" />
```

## Portal

`<Portal>` renders its children at the end of another element. This is useful for modals, toasts and popovers that must escape `overflow: hidden` or stacking contexts:

```html Modal.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { Portal } from '@inflector/keeno'
  import type { Children } from '@inflector/keeno'
  const { onClose, children } = props<{ onClose: () => void; children?: Children }>()
</script>

<Portal target="body">
  <div class="backdrop" onClick={onClose}>
    <div class="modal" onClick={(e) => e.stopPropagation()}>{children?.()}</div>
  </div>
</Portal>

<style>
  .backdrop { position: fixed; inset: 0; background: rgb(0 0 0 / 0.4) }
</style>
```

- `target` is an element or a CSS selector. It defaults to `document.body`, and is read once, when the portal is created.
- The children stay part of this component: its scoped styles, context, error boundaries and `destroy` all apply, and their nodes are removed when the portal is destroyed.
- With `renderToString`, portal content is appended after the app's HTML, each portal in a `<div data-keeno-portal="…">` (the selector, if `target` was one). `hydrate` replaces it and renders the portal at its target.
- DOM events bubble through the real DOM, that is through the target and not through the portal's position in the tree.

## reparentable

`reparentable()` renders content once and lets you show it in different places while it keeps its state: the same component instances and the same DOM nodes move, instead of being destroyed in one place and created again in another. Put the handle in markup wherever the content should appear now:

```html Lesson.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { reparentable } from '@inflector/keeno'
  import Video from './Video.kn'
  const { src } = props<{ src: string }>()
  const theater = state(false)
  const player = reparentable(() => <Video src={src} />)
</script>

{theater ? <dialog open class="theater">{player}</dialog> : <aside class="inline">{player}</aside>}
<button onClick={() => theater.set(!theater)}>Theater mode</button>
```

In browsers with the native [`moveBefore`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Element/moveBefore) (Chrome and Edge 133+ and recent Firefox, not yet Safari), the move also keeps what the DOM itself holds: an iframe or a video keeps playing, focus and text selection stay, and CSS animations and transitions continue. Elsewhere the nodes are re-inserted, so component state is kept but an iframe reloads.

- The content is created the first time it is rendered and lives as long as the component that called `reparentable()`, not as long as the place showing it. `player.dispose()` destroys it earlier.
- While it is shown nowhere it stays alive, with its `update` callbacks still running, so it comes back as it was. Show it in one place at a time.
- Context and error boundaries are the ones around the `reparentable()` call. Its scoped styles are those of the component that renders it.
- Called outside a component (in a store module), the content lives until `dispose()`: for example a player that keeps going across route changes.

### Moving it imperatively

Code that works with elements directly, like drag and drop, a layout engine or a picture-in-picture toggle, can move the content itself:

```html Lesson.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { reparentable } from '@inflector/keeno'
  import Video from './Video.kn'
  const player = reparentable(() => <Video src="/intro.mp4" />)

  function dropInto(e: DragEvent) {
    player.moveTo(e.currentTarget as Element)
  }
</script>

<aside>{player}</aside>
<div class="dropzone" onDragover={(e) => e.preventDefault()} onDrop={dropInto}></div>
<button onClick={() => player.moveTo('#pip')}>Picture in picture</button>
<button onClick={() => player.remove()}>Hide</button>
```

- `player.moveTo(target, before?)` moves the content into `target` (an element or a CSS selector), before `before` or at the end. It creates the content if it was never rendered. The move happens right away and is native where the browser supports it. The content stays there and keeps following its own updates.
- `player.remove()` takes the content out of the page. It stays alive and can be shown again as it was.
- `player.nodes()` returns its current nodes, wherever they are, for example to measure them.
- After `moveTo()` or `remove()`, a place in markup that was already showing the content does not take it back just because it updates. A place that renders it anew does, such as a branch of a condition that switches back, and from then on markup is in charge again.

For a single DOM node that isn't Keeno content, `moveNode(node, parent, before?)` does the same native-when-possible move.

For items that move between lists, such as cards on a kanban board, use `keyedReparentable()`. It creates one entry per key on first use, and every entry belongs to the component that called it, even when it is first rendered inside a list row:

```html Board.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { keyedReparentable } from '@inflector/keeno'
  import Card from './Card.kn'
  const cards = state([{ id: 1, column: 'todo' }, { id: 2, column: 'done' }])
  const cardView = keyedReparentable((id: number) => <Card id={id} />)

  function remove(id: number) {
    cards.set(cards.filter((c) => c.id !== id))
    cardView.delete(id)
  }
</script>

{['todo', 'done'].map((column) => (
  <ul key={column}>
    {cards.filter((c) => c.column === column).map((c) => <li key={c.id}>{cardView(c.id)}</li>)}
  </ul>
))}
```

Moving a card to the other column re-creates its `<li>`, but the `<Card>` inside moves with its state. `cardView.delete(id)` destroys an entry and `cardView.keys()` lists the live ones.

## Transition

`<Transition>` animates elements as they are added and removed inside it. Elements that are being removed stay in place until their animation ends.

```html Panel.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { Transition } from '@inflector/keeno'
  const open = state(false)
</script>

<button onClick={() => open.set(!open)}>Toggle</button>
<Transition name="fade">{open && <div class="panel">Hello</div>}</Transition>

<style>
  .fade-enter-active, .fade-leave-active { transition: opacity 200ms }
  .fade-enter-from, .fade-leave-to { opacity: 0 }
</style>
```

An entering element gets the classes `{name}-enter-from` and `{name}-enter-active` first. One frame later, `{name}-enter-from` is swapped for `{name}-enter-to`, and all three are removed when the longest transition or animation on the element ends. Leaving works the same way with `leave`. The default `name` is `keeno`.

- `appear`: also animate the elements present on first render.
- `onEnter(el, done)` / `onLeave(el, done)`: animate with JavaScript (for example the Web Animations API) instead of classes. Call `done()` when finished.
- This works for conditionals, ternaries (the old and new element animate at the same time) and keyed lists.
- A dynamic `class={…}` on an animated element replaces its class list, which drops the transition classes. Animate a wrapper element instead.

---

<!-- file: docs/routing.md -->

# Routing

`@inflector/keeno-router` is a small client-side router built on the History API. It comes with the Vite plugin (`@inflector/vite-plugin-keeno`), so with Vite there is nothing more to install: import from `@inflector/keeno-router` and the plugin resolves it. Install it yourself (`bun add @inflector/keeno-router`) to pin its version, or to use it without the plugin.

The quickest way to use it is [file-based routing](file-routing.md), as `examples/todo` does.

## Routes

```html App.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { lazy } from '@inflector/keeno'
  import { Link, Router, type RouteDefinition } from '@inflector/keeno-router'
  import Home from './Home.kn'
  import User from './User.kn'
  import NotFound from './NotFound.kn'

  const routes: RouteDefinition[] = [
    { path: '/', component: Home },
    { path: '/users/:id', component: User },
    { path: '/settings', component: lazy(() => import('./Settings.kn')) },
    { path: '*', component: NotFound },
  ]
</script>

<nav>
  <Link href="/" exact>Home</Link>
  <Link href="/users/1">Ada</Link>
  <Link href="/settings">Settings</Link>
</nav>
<Router routes={routes} />
```

- Routes are tried in order and the first match wins, so put specific paths before general ones and `*` last.
- `:name` matches one path segment. A final `*` matches the rest of the path, as `params['*']`, and `*name` names it, as `params.name`. Trailing slashes are ignored and params are URL-decoded.
- `<Router>` keeps the component when only the params change, so `/users/1` → `/users/2` updates `params` in place. It creates a new instance when a different route matches.
- `fallback={() => …}` renders when nothing matches, if you don't want a `*` route.
- `base="/app"` serves the app under a path prefix. Route paths, `<Link href>` and `navigate()` then use paths without the prefix.

## Route components

A route component receives `params`:

```html User.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { useRoute } from '@inflector/keeno-router'
  const { params } = props<{ params: { id: string } }>()
  const route = useRoute()
</script>

<h1>User {params.id}</h1>
<p>Tab: {route.query.get('tab') ?? 'overview'}</p>
```

`useRoute()` gives the current route anywhere inside `<Router>`: `path`, `params`, `query` (a `URLSearchParams`), `hash` and `matched` (the route definition). Its fields are reactive, so templates and `update()` follow navigation.

## Navigation

- `<Link href="/users/1">` renders an `<a>` that navigates without reloading. While its path is active, it gets the class `active` (change it with `activeClass`) and `aria-current="page"`. A link is active on its own path and on the paths below it, and `exact` limits it to its own path. `replace` replaces the history entry instead of adding one.
- The scoped styles of the component that renders a `<Link>` apply to its `<a>`: `a { … }` and `.active { … }` in that component's `<style>` reach it.
- To write your own anchor, use the `link` click handler: `<a href="/about" onClick={link}>About</a>`. With a `base`, write `href={href('/about')}`. `isActive('/about')` tells you whether to mark it.
- `navigate('/users/2')` navigates from code. `navigate('/login', { replace: true })` replaces the current entry, and `{ scroll: false }` keeps the scroll position. A URL with a `#hash` scrolls to that element instead of the top. On back/forward, the router restores the scroll position the page had, once the route has rendered. Relative URLs such as `navigate('?tab=2')` work too.
- Clicks with a modifier key, a middle click, `target="_blank"`, `download` and links to other sites are left to the browser.
- Query parameters synced with `state(v, { url: 'tab' })` follow navigation, including back and forward.

## View transitions

`<Router viewTransition>` animates navigations with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API): links, `navigate()`, and back and forward. By default the browser cross-fades the old page into the new one. Browsers without the API navigate as usual.

```html App.kn
<Router routes={routes} viewTransition />
```

- One navigation can opt out with `navigate(to, { transition: false })`, or opt in without the router default with `navigate(to, { transition: true })`, `<Link transition>` or `<a data-transition onClick={link}>`.
- The new page is rendered inside the transition, so code right after `navigate()` still sees the old route until the browser starts the transition.
- Give an element the same `view-transition-name` on both pages to animate it from one position to the other, for example a thumbnail that grows into a hero image:

```html
<!-- List.kn -->
<img src={photo.thumb} style={`view-transition-name: photo-${photo.id}`} />

<!-- Photo.kn -->
<img src={photo.full} style={`view-transition-name: photo-${photo.id}`} />
```

Customize the animation with the `::view-transition-*` pseudo-elements, and respect users who prefer less motion:

```css
::view-transition-old(root),
::view-transition-new(root) {
  animation-duration: 200ms;
}

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  ::view-transition-group(*),
  ::view-transition-old(*),
  ::view-transition-new(*) {
    animation: none !important;
  }
}
```

Put this CSS in a global stylesheet, or inside `:global()` in a component's `<style>`.

## File-based routing

With the Vite plugin, the routes can come from the files in `src/pages` instead: `about.kn` is `/about`, `[id].kn` is `/:id`, with `_layout.kn`, `_404.kn` and `_500.kn` for layouts and error pages. See [File-based routing](file-routing.md).

## Server rendering

On the server there is no browser location, so pass the request URL: `<Router routes={routes} url={request.url} />`. See [Server rendering](ssr.md).

---

<!-- file: docs/file-routing.md -->

# File-based Routing

With the Vite plugin, the files in `src/pages` are your routes: `about.kn` is `/about`, `users/[id].kn` is `/users/:id`, and `_layout.kn` wraps the pages next to it. There is no route table to keep in sync, and nothing to install beyond `@inflector/vite-plugin-keeno`, which comes with the [router](routing.md).

## Setup

File routing is on by default. These are the defaults, written out:

```ts vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import keeno from '@inflector/vite-plugin-keeno'

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [keeno({ useFileRouter: true, pages: './src/pages' })],
})
```

Mount the `Pages` component of `virtual:keeno-pages`. It renders the page for the current URL, inside its layouts:

```ts main.ts
import { mount } from '@inflector/keeno'
import Pages from 'virtual:keeno-pages'

mount(Pages, document.getElementById('app')!)
```

For TypeScript, reference the plugin's client types once, in any `.d.ts` file:

```ts env.d.ts
/// <reference types="@inflector/vite-plugin-keeno/client" />
```

| Option | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `useFileRouter` | `true` | Provide `virtual:keeno-pages`. `false` turns it off. |
| `pages` | `'./src/pages'` | The pages directory, relative to the Vite root. It must be inside the root. |

## Files and routes

```
src/pages/
├── _layout.kn        layout around every page
├── _404.kn           no page matches
├── _500.kn           a page threw an error
├── index.kn          /
├── about.kn          /about
├── users/
│   ├── _layout.kn    layout around the users pages, inside the root one
│   ├── index.kn      /users
│   ├── new.kn        /users/new
│   └── [id].kn       /users/:id
└── docs/
    ├── intro.kn      /docs/intro
    └── _all.kn       anything else below /docs
```

| File | Route |
|---|---|
| `index.kn` | The directory's own path: `index.kn` is `/`, `users/index.kn` is `/users`. |
| `about.kn` | `/about`. Directories add segments: `blog/latest.kn` is `/blog/latest`. |
| `[id].kn` | One segment, as `params.id`. Directories work too: `users/[id]/posts.kn` is `/users/:id/posts`. |
| `_all.kn` | Every path below its directory that no other page matches, as `params['*']`. |
| `_layout.kn` | Wraps the pages of its directory and of the directories below it. |
| `_404.kn` | Paths below its directory that match nothing. |
| `_500.kn`, `_403.kn`, … | Errors with that HTTP status, thrown while a page renders. |

The most specific route wins, whatever the order of the files: static segments before `[param]`s, and `[param]`s before `_all`. So `users/new.kn` matches `/users/new` and `users/[id].kn` matches every other `/users/…`.

Files and directories whose names start with `_` and that aren't one of the special files above are not routes. Keep a page's own components next to it, as `users/_Avatar.kn` or `users/_components/`.

## Pages

A page is an ordinary component. It receives `params`, and `useRoute()` gives it the query string and the rest of the route:

```html users/[id].kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { useRoute } from '@inflector/keeno-router'
  const { params } = props<{ params: { id: string } }>()
  const route = useRoute()
</script>

<h1>User {params.id}</h1>
<p>Tab: {route.query.get('tab') ?? 'overview'}</p>
```

Moving from `/users/1` to `/users/2` keeps the page and updates `params` in place, so write anything that depends on them reactively (in the template, `derived` or `update`).

Pages load on demand: each one is its own chunk, fetched the first time it is shown. Layouts and error pages are bundled with the routes, so they never wait.

Link between pages with `<Link>` and `navigate()`, as described in [Routing](routing.md#navigation).

## Layouts

A `_layout.kn` receives `params` and `children`, and renders `{children}` where the page goes:

```html _layout.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import type { Children } from '@inflector/keeno'
  import { Link } from '@inflector/keeno-router'
  const { children } = props<{ children: Children }>()
</script>

<nav>
  <Link href="/" exact>Home</Link>
  <Link href="/users">Users</Link>
</nav>
<main>{children}</main>

<style>
  .active { font-weight: 600 }
</style>
```

- Layouts nest. A page in `users/` renders inside `users/_layout.kn`, which renders inside `_layout.kn`.
- A layout stays mounted while you navigate between pages that share it. Only what changes below it is replaced, so the root layout is your app shell: its state, its DOM, a playing video or a scroll position in a sidebar survive navigation.
- `params` follows the URL, so a layout in `users/[id]/` can show the user while its pages switch between tabs.

## Not found and error pages

A path that matches no page renders the closest `_404.kn`: for `/users/1/nope`, `users/_404.kn` if there is one, else `_404.kn`. It renders inside the layouts of its directory. Without any `_404.kn`, nothing is rendered.

A page can show an error page itself by throwing `httpError(status)`:

```html users/[id].kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { httpError } from '@inflector/keeno-router'
  const { params } = props<{ params: { id: string } }>()
  if (!/^\d+$/.test(params.id)) throw httpError(404, `No user ${params.id}`)
</script>

<h1>User {params.id}</h1>
```

Any other error thrown while the page renders (including in `init` and `update`) is a 500. The page for that status comes from the closest directory that has one, and renders inside the page's layouts. If there is none, the error goes on to the closest [`<ErrorBoundary>`](built-ins.md#errorboundary), or to `mount()`.

Error pages receive `status`, `error`, `params` and `reset`:

```html _500.kn
<script lang="ts">
  const { status, error, reset } = props<{ status: number; error: unknown; reset: () => void }>()
</script>

<h1>Error {status}</h1>
<p>{error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error)}</p>
<button onClick={reset}>Try again</button>
```

`reset()` renders the page again, and navigating to another path clears the error. As with `<ErrorBoundary>`, errors in event handlers, timers and promises don't happen while rendering, so they don't show an error page: store them in a state and throw it from the template if they should. `errorStatus(error)` gives the status a thrown value maps to.

## Server rendering

Pass the request URL as `url`. Pages load on demand and rendering is synchronous, so load the page first with `preloadRoute()`, on the server and again in the browser before hydrating:

```ts entry-server.ts
import { renderToString } from '@inflector/keeno/server'
import { preloadRoute } from '@inflector/keeno-router'
import Pages, { routes } from 'virtual:keeno-pages'

export async function render(url: string) {
  await preloadRoute(routes, url)
  return renderToString(Pages, { url })
}
```

```ts entry-client.ts
import { hydrate } from '@inflector/keeno'
import { preloadRoute } from '@inflector/keeno-router'
import Pages, { routes } from 'virtual:keeno-pages'

await preloadRoute(routes, location.pathname)
hydrate(Pages, document.getElementById('app')!)
```

See [Server rendering](ssr.md) for the rest of the setup.

## Without the plugin's module

`virtual:keeno-pages` also exports `routes`, the generated route definitions, to pass to your own `<Router>`:

```html App.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { Router } from '@inflector/keeno-router'
  import { routes } from 'virtual:keeno-pages'
</script>

<Router routes={routes} base="/app" />
```

`Pages` itself takes the other props of `<Router>`, such as `<Pages base="/app" />`.

The routes come from `pageRoutes()`, which works with any `import.meta.glob` of `.kn` files:

```ts
import { pageRoutes } from '@inflector/keeno-router'

const routes = pageRoutes(import.meta.glob('/src/pages/**/*.kn'), '/src/pages')
```

Hand-written routes can use the same features: a `RouteDefinition` takes `layouts` (outermost first) and `errors` (error pages by status).

```ts
const routes: RouteDefinition[] = [
  { path: '/', component: Home, layouts: [Shell], errors: { 404: NotFound, 500: Oops } },
]
```

---

<!-- file: docs/ssr.md -->

# Server rendering

Keeno renders components to HTML on the server (Node, Bun or Deno) with `renderToString`. In the browser, `hydrate` then takes over that markup.

```bash
bun add linkedom
```

`renderToString` creates nodes with [linkedom](https://github.com/WebReflection/linkedom), a small server-side DOM, so it needs that package installed. It doesn't change any globals.

## Rendering

```ts
// src/entry-server.ts
import { renderToString } from '@inflector/keeno/server'
import App from './App.kn'

export async function render(url: string) {
  return renderToString(App, { url })
}
```

```ts
// src/entry-client.ts
import { hydrate } from '@inflector/keeno'
import App from './App.kn'

hydrate(App, document.getElementById('app')!)
```

What runs on the server:

- The `<script>` block, templates, `derived` values and child components render, and text and attributes are escaped.
- `init` and `update` callbacks **don't** run, because there is no mounted DOM. Put browser-only code (`window`, `localStorage`, timers, fetching in the browser) in `init`.
- [Async deriveds](reactivity.md#async-derived) are awaited: the HTML contains their values, not the `<Loading>` fallback. See [Data](#data) below.
- `<Await>` and `lazy()` render their pending content.
- `state(v, { persist })` and `state(v, { url })` use their initial value.
- `<Transition>` doesn't animate.
- Input values are written as `value="…"` attributes, so they show before the page hydrates.

## Data

`renderToString` waits for the async deriveds the page reads, then returns the HTML with their values, plus a `<script type="application/json" data-keeno-data>` holding them:

```html Post.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import { Loading } from '@inflector/keeno'
  const { id } = props<{ id: string }>()
  const post = derived(async ({ signal }) => (await fetch(`https://api.example.com/posts/${id}`, { signal })).json())
</script>

<Loading fallback={() => <p>Loading…</p>}>
  <h1>{post.title}</h1>
</Loading>
```

- `hydrate` reads that script, and each async derived starts with the value the server fetched, so the page doesn't flash a fallback or wait for the data again. The function still runs once to know what it depends on, with an already-aborted `signal`, so a `fetch` given `signal` never reaches the network. Without `signal`, the request is made and its result ignored.
- Values must be JSON-serializable. `derived(fn, { ssr: false })` keeps a value out of the HTML (the browser fetches it).
- Values are matched by the order async deriveds first run, which is the same on the server and in the browser for the same props and URL. `derived(fn, { key: 'post' })` names one explicitly.
- `renderToString(App, props, { timeout })` stops waiting after `timeout` ms (default 10 000). What's still loading renders its fallback and is fetched in the browser.

## Streaming

`renderToStream(App, props)` returns a `ReadableStream<string>`. The first chunk is the page with each waiting `<Loading>` showing its fallback, so the browser can paint right away. Each boundary's content follows as soon as its data is ready, and a small inline script swaps it in place of the fallback.

```ts
// Bun or any runtime with web streams
import { renderToStream } from '@inflector/keeno/server'
import App from './App.kn'

Bun.serve({
  async fetch(req) {
    const app = renderToStream(App, { url: req.url })
    const head = '<!doctype html><html><head><script type="module" src="/entry-client.js"></script></head><body><div id="app">'
    const tail = '</div></body></html>'
    const body = app.pipeThrough(
      new TransformStream<string, string>({
        start: (c) => c.enqueue(head),
        flush: (c) => c.enqueue(tail),
      }),
    ).pipeThrough(new TextEncoderStream())
    return new Response(body, { headers: { 'content-type': 'text/html; charset=utf-8' } })
  },
})
```

- Load the client entry with `<script type="module">`: module scripts run after the document has finished loading, so `hydrate` sees the complete page.
- Nested boundaries stream independently. One that is ready before the boundary around it goes out with it.
- Portals render with the first chunk; a portal inside a streamed boundary appears when the page hydrates.

## Hydration

`hydrate(App, element, props)` renders the app in the browser and replaces the server markup in the same task, so nothing flashes. It is simpler than node-by-node hydration, but has some costs:

- The client renders the whole tree once, so the page becomes interactive no faster than with `mount()`.
- Focus, text selection and text typed into inputs before `hydrate` runs are lost. Keep the time between first paint and hydration short: load the client script with `<script type="module">` in `<head>`.
- If the client render throws, the server markup stays and the error is rethrown.

## With Vite

Set up Vite's SSR mode as the [Vite SSR guide](https://vite.dev/guide/ssr) describes. `@inflector/vite-plugin-keeno` needs no extra options.

- **In development**, load your server entry with `vite.ssrLoadModule('/src/entry-server.ts')`. Don't import `renderToString` directly in your Node server file. The components and `renderToString` must come from the same copy of the runtime, and the runtime warns when two copies are loaded.
- **In production**, build the client with `vite build`, then the server entry with `vite build --ssr src/entry-server.ts`, and import the server bundle from Node.
- Scoped CSS is part of the client build. Link the CSS files from Vite's manifest in your HTML template, as the Vite guide describes.

## Routing

On the server, give the router the request URL: `<Router routes={routes} url={url} />`, with `url` a prop of your app that only `entry-server` passes. On the client `url` is `undefined`, so the router follows the browser location. See [Routing](routing.md).

## Without Vite

`renderToStringWith(document, App, props)` renders synchronously with a DOM document you provide, for example another server DOM implementation, or a test.

---

<!-- file: docs/security.md -->

# Security

## What is escaped

- `{expr}` in markup always renders as text (a DOM text node), never as HTML. `<p>{userInput}</p>` is safe whatever `userInput` contains.
- Attribute values are set with `setAttribute` or the matching DOM property. They can't break out of the attribute.
- Static text and attributes written in a template are escaped by the compiler.
- `renderToString` escapes text and attributes in the HTML it produces.

## What is not

**`innerHTML`.** `<div innerHTML={html} />` inserts raw HTML, exactly like the DOM property. Never pass it content that a user can influence unless you sanitize it first, for example with [DOMPurify](https://github.com/cure53/DOMPurify):

```html Article.kn
<script lang="ts">
  import DOMPurify from 'dompurify'
  const { body } = props<{ body: string }>()
</script>

<article innerHTML={DOMPurify.sanitize(body)} />
```

**`javascript:` URLs.** A dynamic URL attribute (`href`, `src`, `action`, `formaction`, `xlink:href`, `poster`, `cite`, `background`, `ping`) whose value is a `javascript:` URL is **blocked**: the attribute is removed and an error is logged. Browsers also accept variants with leading spaces, tabs inside the scheme and mixed case, and those are blocked too. A static `href="javascript:…"` written in the template is left alone, since the author wrote it. Other schemes, such as `data:` URLs in `src`, pass through. Validate them yourself if users can supply them.

**`srcdoc`.** `<iframe srcdoc={html} />` renders `html` as a whole document, like `innerHTML`. Sanitize user content, or keep the iframe's `sandbox` without `allow-same-origin`.

**Event handlers and spread.** `{...attrs}` applies every key as an attribute, except keys like `onClick` or `onclick`: a function there becomes an event listener, and anything else is ignored. A dynamic inline handler attribute (`onclick={…}` as a string, from a spread or a binding) is never set. Still, don't spread objects that come from users.

**Styles.** A `style={…}` string that comes from user input can still do things like overlay the page. Prefer fixed classes.

## Content Security Policy

The runtime and compiled components don't use `eval`, `new Function` or inline event handler attributes. They work under a strict CSP such as `script-src 'self'`. In development, Vite injects styles with `<style>` tags, so `style-src` needs `'unsafe-inline'` or a nonce there. Production builds emit CSS files.

Templates are parsed once per component by assigning the compiler's static HTML to a `<template>` element's `innerHTML`. A page that enforces [Trusted Types](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Trusted_Types_API) (`require-trusted-types-for 'script'`) needs a default policy that allows those assignments.

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please report security issues privately through [GitHub security advisories](https://github.com/iliesw/Keeno/security/advisories/new), not in public issues.
